english_translation: I will wake up in the morning to wash all the remaining clothes.

dialogue.shona: Ndichamuka mangwanani kuti ndiwache hembe dzose dzasara.
dialogue.english: I will wake up in the morning to wash all the remaining clothes.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndichamuka [I will muka] • mangwanani [good morning / morning] • kuti [that / so that] • ndiwache [ndiwache] • hembe [shirt / garment] • dzose [dzose] • dzasara [dzasara]

grammar_notes.title: Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('mangwanani')
grammar_notes.content: In this lesson you encounter 'mangwanani'. Shona greetings change depending on the time of day and how many people you are addressing. 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning, 'Masikati' in the afternoon, and 'Manheru' in the evening. For a casual 'Hello' to a friend or peer, use 'Mhoro' (or 'Mhoroi' when speaking politely to an elder or group). To ask 'How are you?', speakers use 'Makadini?' (polite/plural) or ask how your day went with 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?').
grammar_notes.rule: Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Future with '-cha-' ('Ndichamuka')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'Ndichamuka' in this sentence. Whenever you want to say what 'will' happen in the future, simply place the future marker '-cha-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem. For example, 'ndichabika' means 'I will cook', 'tichasvika' means 'we will arrive', and 'mvura ichanaya' means 'the rain will fall'. Pair it with 'mangwana' ('tomorrow') to talk about tomorrow's plans!
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -cha- + Verb Stem = Future ('will') -> Ndichaenda (I will go), Vachadzoka (They will return)

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

cultural_notes.title: Early Morning Laundry ('Kuwacha Hembe') & Sunshine Drying
cultural_notes.content: In most Zimbabwean households, washing clothes ('kuwacha hembe') is done early in the morning ('mangwanani') so that garments hung on the outdoor washing line ('waya yembatya') catch the full warmth of the morning sun and breeze.

active_exercises.prompt: You meet your neighbour at 7:00 PM in the evening. Which greeting is appropriate?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Manheru' is the greeting used in the evening, paired with 'makadini henyu?' ('how are you?').

active_exercises.prompt: Your friend just passed her driving test! What do you say to congratulate her in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Makorokoto!' means 'Congratulations!' and 'nekubudirira kwako' means 'on your success'.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this future weather forecast: 'Mangwana zuva ______ zvakanaka.' (Tomorrow the sun will shine brightly.)
active_exercises.explanation: 'Zuva' (sun) takes the prefix 'ri-' + future marker '-cha-' + '-buda' (come out/shine) -> 'richabuda'.
